newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Softer U.S. wheat prices send Manila mills jumping.
newsitem.headline: Softer U.S. wheat prices send Manila mills jumping.

text.p: Manila flour mills are expected to resume buying this week after prices slid overnight on the USDA's report of higher carryover wheat stocks for 1996-1997, local flour executives and grains traders said on Tuesday.
"This is a welcome development. Expect us to jump into the market," an executive in a local mill told Reuters.

Philippine flour mills sent tender invitations for 90,000 tonnes of U.S. wheat last week. Only one mill bought 7,500 tonnes of soft wheat because the other mills received offers higher than expected, a senior trader said.
"Get ready for another round of tenders from other mills which have yet to buy their requirements for June," said another trader.
But not all commodities traders in Manila were happy about the fall of U.S. wheat, corn, soyoil, soybean and soymeal prices overnight due to better-than-expected 1996-1997 carryover stocks.
Philippine vegetable oil traders said the collapse of soybean and soymeal prices would further depress coconut oil prices.
"This is more bad news for coconut oil, coming at a time of rising copra supplies from the Philippines," said a senior trader in one of the country's largest coconut mills.

Prospects of better Philippine coconut harvests in the second half of the year pulled down copra prices to nine pesos per kg from 10.50 the previous weeek. Crude coconut oil also dipped to 16 pesos per kg from the previous 17.30.
The drop in domestic prices of copra and coconut oil will spill over in international markets, traders said.
Coconut Oil Refiners Association president Jesus Arranza said recently he expected Philippine coconut oil exports to rise between 1.2 and 1.3 million tonnes this year against 813,157 tonnes in 1996.
Corn, soymeal and soybean buyers are expected to remain in the sidelines even with lower U.S. prices, traders said.
"We had made orders for our soybean requirement up to June this year," said an executive in a Philippine firm. "For futures orders that we have made earlier, we can peg prices today."
Soymeal buyers said they have ample supplies while local hog and poultry farmers said they were still awaiting government's approval on their proposal to buy 300,000 tonnes of corn for animal feed.
